result: The BASS domain structure was determined to 2.6-Å resolution using X-ray crystallography and validated with structure-based mutagenesis. The structure reveals a novel 26-nm, 260-Å long four-helix bundle consisting of an anti-parallel coiled-coil dimer in the asymmetric unit that associates through a crystallographic dyad to form a tetramer with a ~7000 Å² dimer-dimer interface. The central bundle transitions to an asymmetric diamond-shaped bundle near its ends with helical bends ('elbows'), bringing N-terminal helices into close proximity to emerge as parallel coiled-coil dimers offset by 90°.
evaluation: Claims C38-C60 collectively describe the crystallographic structure determination and key structural features of the BASS domain. The 2.6-Å resolution structure (C43), crystallographic data (C42), EM validation (C41, C51), and detailed structural measurements (C47, C49) provide strong experimental support. The novel structural organization (C59) is well-documented through multiple figures and is consistent with previous biochemical data (C60).

result: The central bundle of the BASS tetramer displays a unique alternating pattern of hydrophobic and ionic interfaces (A-D) not observed in other four-helix bundles. Each interface occupies approximately three helical turns, with interface A (hydrophobic, Met729/730/733 and Leu725/726) at the center, bracketed by ionic interface B (Arg740-Glu715/722, Lys737-Asp723), hydrophobic interface C (Leu705/708/712 with Met747/Leu751/Met754), and ionic interface D (Arg761-Asp701) at the elbows. These interfaces are conserved across Kinesin-5 orthologs and stabilize the tetrameric assembly.
evaluation: Claims C5-C77 and C107 describe the detailed molecular architecture of the central bundle interfaces. The structural data from the crystal structure (Figures 5, 6) clearly show the alternating hydrophobic/ionic pattern, specific residue interactions, and conservation across species (Figure 7). The novelty claim (C63, C77) is supported by comparisons to other structures (Figure 3). The seven interfaces provide a comprehensive structural basis for tetramer assembly.

result: N-terminal BASS helices undergo a helix-swapping transition mediated by 10° bends at Pro699 and Gly693 ('elbows'), transitioning from anti-parallel to parallel coiled-coils at both ends with a 90° rotational offset. This swap is mediated by hydrophobic interface E (Met687/Leu691/Leu694 with Met768/Ile772) and di-tyrosine interface F (Tyr775-Tyr775 with His683 π-π stacking). Beyond interface F, N-terminal helices form parallel coiled-coils (residues 640-670) stabilized by heptad packing with Phe669-Phe669 π-π interactions.
evaluation: Claims C9-C93 and C108 describe the helix-swapping mechanism at the BASS domain ends. The crystal structure (Figures 4, 6) clearly shows the helical bends, interface details, and 90° offset. Specific residues mediating the swap (C82-C92) are well-resolved in the structure. Conservation of key residues (C87, C92) supports functional importance. The parallel coiled-coil formation (C88-C93) is structurally validated.

result: Structure-based mutagenesis validates the critical role of alternating hydrophobic and ionic interfaces in BASS tetramerization. Single mutations in ionic interfaces B (Arg740) and D (Arg761) cause potent defects producing dimer/tetramer mixtures, while mutations in the parallel coiled-coil region (Phe669Glu) maintain tetrameric state. Multiple interface mutations produce monomeric BASS, demonstrating cumulative roles of both hydrophobic and ionic interfaces in organizing and stabilizing the tetramer.
evaluation: Claims C8, C94-C100 describe mutagenesis experiments validating the structure. The data (Figure 8, Tables 2-3) show clear oligomerization defects for interface mutants, with particularly strong effects for single Arg mutations (C96). The differential effects of mutations in different regions (C96 vs C97) support the structural model. Hydrodynamic analysis (gel filtration, sucrose gradients) provides quantitative validation. The cumulative effects of multiple mutations (C98) further support the model.

result: The authors propose that BASS is a mechanically stable, plectonemically-coiled junction that transmits forces between Kinesin-5 motor dimers during microtubule sliding. The heavily intertwined four-helix bundle is hypothesized to be torsionally stiff, which may be crucial for setting the 90° offset and for mechanically stabilizing the central rod during force transmission.
evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C79, C111-C113, C115-C116 propose mechanical properties and force transmission functions based on structural features. While the plectonemic coiling and intertwined structure are observed (C111), the mechanical stability (C12), torsional stiffness (C112), and force transmission capabilities (C13, C79, C115) are inferences without direct experimental validation. No mechanical measurements or force transmission assays are presented. These remain reasonable but untested hypotheses.

result: A model of the full-length Kinesin-5 central rod was built by superimposing parallel coiled-coils onto the BASS structure. The model indicates that the BASS tetrameric fold dictates long-range structural assembly of N-terminal and C-terminal helical regions, producing head-to-tail junctions at bipolar ends. The C-terminal sequences may not be fully helical due to shorter length compared to N-terminal coiled-coils.
evaluation: Claims C102-C105 describe a molecular model built from the BASS structure (Figure 9). While the model is based on the validated BASS structure, the organization of regions outside BASS (C102-C104) involves significant inference and modeling. The match to EM length (C105) provides some validation, but the authors acknowledge the rod is longer than observed. The C-terminal structure prediction (C104) is speculative. The model is reasonable but requires further experimental validation.

result: The BASS domain orchestrates a parallel organization and 90° rotational offset of motor domain pairs at each end of the Kinesin-5 minifilament, resembling Kinesin-1 organization. This organization may enable processive hand-over-hand motility of adjacent motor domains along each microtubule, allowing the tetramer to slide microtubules outward or constrain their sliding.
evaluation: Claims C58, C109-C110 propose functional consequences of the BASS structure for motor domain organization and motility. While the 90° offset is structurally validated (C11, C55), the functional implications for hand-over-hand motility (C110) and microtubule sliding (C58) are inferences based on comparison to Kinesin-1 and cited literature. No direct motility assays with the BASS structure are presented. These are reasonable hypotheses requiring functional validation.

result: The ionic interfaces B and D are open molecular pockets accessible to small molecules that could potentially serve as drug targets. Small molecules interfering with these ionic interactions could disrupt Kinesin-5 tetramer assembly and function, providing a possible therapeutic strategy for cancer treatment.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81, C101, C124 propose therapeutic applications based on the structure. While the ionic interfaces are structurally characterized (C80) and mutagenesis shows their importance (C96, C101), the drug targeting potential (C81, C124) is entirely speculative. No small molecule screening, binding studies, or cellular assays are presented. This represents a reasonable future direction but lacks experimental support.

result: The 90° offset of the BASS structure could contribute to the motor's observed threefold preference for crosslinking anti-parallel versus parallel microtubules.
evaluation: Claim C114 proposes a structural explanation for the known MT orientation preference (C22). While the 90° offset is structurally validated (C11, C55), the connection to MT orientation preference is speculative. The authors acknowledge 'further work is required to test this idea.' No experiments testing this hypothesis are presented.

result: No evidence was obtained for assembly of Kinesin-5 tetramers into higher order oligomers. The extensive intertwining of the four chains makes dissociation into dimers during force transmission unlikely, suggesting the bipolar tetramer represents the functional unit of Kinesin-5 activity.
evaluation: Claims C117-C119 describe negative results and inferences about oligomerization state. The lack of higher-order oligomers (C117) is supported by gel filtration and EM data (Figures 1, 8). The inference about dissociation resistance (C118) is reasonable based on the extensive intertwining observed in the structure. The conclusion about the functional unit (C119) is consistent with cited motility assays, though not directly tested here.

result: The BASS domain structure differs from the previously proposed antiparallel arrangement of two side-by-side parallel coiled-coils and may represent a new class of force-pliable four-helical anti-parallel junctions capable of orienting dimeric coiled-coils in opposite directions.
evaluation: Claims C40 and C61 contrast the new structure with previous models. The structural data clearly shows the novel four-helix bundle organization (C5-C7, C107) differs from earlier predictions (cited in C40). The proposal of a new structural class (C61) is reasonable given the unique features (C63, C77) but remains somewhat speculative without identification of other members of this class.

result: The BASS structure is the first atomic structure of a kinesin superfamily oligomerization domain. Conservation of sequence, structural features, and length among Kinesin-5 family members suggests the BASS properties are key to understanding Kinesin-5 function across organisms.
evaluation: Claims C106 and C120 make comparative statements about the field. The novelty claim (C106) appears accurate based on knowledge of kinesin structures. The conservation analysis (C120) is supported by sequence alignments (Figure 7) showing conservation of key interface residues across species. The inference about functional importance is reasonable given the conservation data.

result: The bipolar organization of Kinesin-5 resembles myosin-2 filaments, but unlike variable-length myosin-2 filaments, the BASS domain organizes four Kinesin-5 subunits into stable, mechanically robust bipolar tetramers of uniform length capable of bearing compressive and tensile forces.
evaluation: Claims C121-C123 compare Kinesin-5 to myosin-2. The structural comparison (C121) is reasonable and supported by citations. The myosin-2 properties (C122) are established knowledge. However, the mechanical properties attributed to BASS (C123) - mechanical robustness, force-bearing capacity - are inferred from structure without direct experimental validation. No mechanical measurements are presented.
